clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of chylomicron clearance, most often from biallelic loss-of-function variants in LPL, or in its cofactors/regulators APOC2, APOA5, GPIHBP1 and LMF1.
Presents from infancy or childhood with grossly elevated fasting triglycerides producing lactescent (milky) serum that may separate into a creamy supernatant layer on standing.
The dominant clinical threat is recurrent acute pancreatitis, which can be severe, necrotising and life-threatening.
Eruptive xanthomata over extensor surfaces and buttocks, lipaemia retinalis and hepatosplenomegaly reflect tissue chylomicron deposition.
Triglyceride elevation is chylomicron-driven and characteristically refractory to fibrates, statins and omega-3 agents, which act mainly on VLDL.
Lifelong severe dietary fat restriction is the cornerstone of management; medium-chain triglycerides are absorbed via the portal vein and bypass chylomicron formation.
Distinguish from the far commoner multifactorial chylomicronaemia, where a milder polygenic and secondary picture allows residual lipolytic capacity and better drug response.
APOC2 deficiency can be unmasked functionally because patient plasma fails to activate lipoprotein lipase unless normal apoC-II is supplied in vitro.
reference.pathophysiology: Familial chylomicronaemia syndrome arises from a near-complete failure of the intravascular lipolytic pathway that normally clears triglyceride-rich chylomicrons. Lipoprotein lipase, anchored at the capillary endothelial luminal surface, hydrolyses chylomicron and VLDL triglyceride, releasing free fatty acids for tissue uptake; its activity requires apolipoprotein C-II as an obligate activator, apolipoprotein A-V to promote lipoprotein docking, GPIHBP1 to bind and shuttle the enzyme to the endothelial surface, and LMF1 for correct enzyme maturation and folding. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in any of these genes abolish effective lipolysis, so ingested fat, packaged into chylomicrons by the gut, accumulates unchecked in plasma along with their remnants, driving fasting triglycerides to extreme concentrations. The resulting hyperviscous, chylomicron-laden plasma is thought to impair pancreatic capillary perfusion and to liberate cytotoxic free fatty acids and lysolecithin locally, precipitating acute pancreatitis, while chylomicron uptake by tissue macrophages produces eruptive xanthomata and hepatosplenomegaly. Because LDL cholesterol is typically normal or low and the defect is confined to triglyceride-rich particle clearance, accelerated atherosclerosis is not the defining hazard, distinguishing the condition mechanistically from the mixed and remnant dyslipidaemias.
additionalDifferentials: Multifactorial (polygenic) chylomicronaemia with secondary aggravation by alcohol, uncontrolled diabetes or oestrogens
Familial hypertriglyceridaemia and familial combined hyperlipidaemia
Familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia (type III) with mixed remnant accumulation
Secondary severe hypertriglyceridaemia from nephrotic syndrome or hypothyroidism
Drug-induced hypertriglyceridaemia (retinoids, corticosteroids, protease inhibitors, second-generation antipsychotics)
Lipodystrophy syndromes with insulin resistance and hypertriglyceridaemia
Glycogen storage disease type I presenting with hypertriglyceridaemia in childhood
additionalInvestigations: Fasting lipid profile confirming grossly elevated triglycerides with the refrigerator test showing a creamy chylomicron layer
Genetic panel sequencing LPL, APOC2, APOA5, GPIHBP1 and LMF1 for biallelic pathogenic variants
Post-heparin plasma lipoprotein lipase activity and mass assay to demonstrate absent or markedly reduced function
In vitro activation study adding exogenous apoC-II to patient plasma when APOC2 deficiency is suspected
Serum lipase and amylase with cross-sectional pancreatic imaging during suspected pancreatitis
Exclusion of secondary contributors with glucose/HbA1c, thyroid function, renal profile and urinalysis
Assessment of GPIHBP1 autoantibodies where an acquired chylomicronaemia phenotype is suspected
redFlags: Severe abdominal pain with vomiting signalling acute or necrotising pancreatitis
Recurrent pancreatitis episodes indicating inadequate triglyceride control and risk of chronic pancreatic insufficiency
Neonatal or infantile presentation with failure to thrive and lactescent blood samples
Signs of systemic inflammatory response or organ dysfunction during a pancreatitis flare
Confusion or focal neurological features raising concern for hyperviscosity-related complications
reference.prognosis: With rigorous lifelong dietary fat restriction and avoidance of aggravating factors, many patients avoid recurrent pancreatitis and have a normal lifespan, though quality of life is affected by dietary burden. Prognosis worsens where control is poor, with cumulative pancreatic damage, exocrine and endocrine insufficiency, and the risk of fatal necrotising pancreatitis.
pitfalls: Expecting standard triglyceride-lowering drugs to work; the chylomicron-driven defect is largely unresponsive to fibrates, statins and omega-3 preparations.
Attributing extreme triglycerides solely to diet or diabetes and missing an underlying monogenic cause in a young patient.
Spuriously abnormal laboratory results (pseudohyponatraemia, interfered assays) caused by intense lipaemia if plasma is not clarified.
Overlooking the diagnosis when triglycerides are transiently lower during acute illness, fasting or pregnancy fat restriction.
Failing to counsel on alcohol, oestrogen-containing contraception and pregnancy, each of which can precipitate dangerous flares.
references: Standard clinical lipidology and metabolic medicine textbooks
National and international familial chylomicronaemia and severe hypertriglyceridaemia guidelines
management: Lifelong severe dietary fat restriction as the cornerstone, substituting medium-chain triglycerides which bypass chylomicron formation
Supplement fat-soluble vitamins and essential fatty acids to offset the restricted diet
Avoid aggravating factors including alcohol and oestrogen-containing agents, and optimise any coexisting diabetes
Recognise that conventional agents (fibrates, statins, omega-3) are largely ineffective, and consider apolipoprotein C-III-directed therapy such as volanesorsen where available
Prompt inpatient management of acute pancreatitis with fasting, fluid resuscitation and analgesia
Regular monitoring of fasting triglycerides to guide and reinforce dietary adherence
Genetic counselling and family testing given autosomal recessive inheritance
Specialist lipid and metabolic clinic care with dedicated dietitian input
